writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, what steps he is taking to protect consumers in Scotland from subscription traps.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government is committed to protecting consumers across the UK, including in Scotland, from subscription traps. The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 introduces new protections to give consumers greater transparency and control over subscription contracts. These include clearer information before entering a contract, reminders before certain renewal payments, cooling-off rights, and straightforward arrangements for cancelling subscriptions. We anticipate these measures will provide £436 million of consumer benefit per year.

Subject to Parliamentary approval, the new regime will come into force on 1 January 2027. Guidance has also been produced to help businesses prepare for and comply with the new requirements.
writtenQuestions.heading: Internet: Subscriptions

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, what assessment he has made of the potential impact of Royal Mail's new delivery model entitled DM26 on older and digitally excluded residents in rural communities, including those who rely on timely postal communications.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government remains committed to ensuring a reliable and accessible universal postal service for users across the UK, including in rural areas.

Ofcom’s changes to Royal Mail’s USO requirements are intended to meet customer needs, improve reliability of postal services and safeguard the long-term future of the universal postal service. Realising those benefits depends on Royal Mail implementing the reforms operationally through its new delivery model, agreed with the Communication Workers Union (CWU).

The Secretary of State and I met Royal Mail and the CWU on 3 November 2026, stressing the importance of management and the workforce working together constructively to improve the service going forward.
writtenQuestions.heading: Postal Services: Rural Areas

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, whether he has considered protections for workers in AI frontier companies who public raise concerns for AI safety in these powerful organisations.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
To qualify for whistleblowing protection under the Employment Rights Act 1996, a worker must reasonably believe that their disclosure tends to show one or more of the types of wrongdoing listed in the Act. These include criminal offences, breaches of legal obligations, and risks to health and safety.

The government has not made a specific assessment of the protections for workers in frontier AI companies who raise concerns about AI safety. However, it is currently consulting on whether the existing categories of wrongdoing remain appropriate, including in relation to emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. The consultation closes on 8 January.
writtenQuestions.heading: Artificial Intelligence: Safety

writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
An assessment of domestic production of virgin polyethylene terephthalate and demand for its use in packaging materials was undertaken as part of the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA) published recommendation to apply a provisional global safeguard measure on 23 October. The recommendation includes further analysis on the likely economic impact a safeguard measure would have on the UK’s economy, including downstream industry, consumers and importers.

The Secretary of State is considering the recommendation and relevant matters in the public interest. His decision on whether to impose a provisional safeguard measure will be announced in due course. I cannot comment further as to do so may prejudice that decision.
writtenQuestions.heading: Plastics: Packaging

At the UK-EU Summit on 20 November 2026, the UK and EU committed to expedite negotiations on a UK-EU architects recognition arrangement and work together to explore recognition arrangements for other professions. The UK government encourages and supports all UK regulators to use the Trade and Cooperation Agreement framework to pursue mutual routes for recognition.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what discussions she has had with Ofcom regarding evidence submitted to the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee on 10 November 2026 on whether platforms are giving sufficient weight to freedom of expression when implementing duties under the Online Safety Act 2023.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, whether the Government Digital Service holds a record of the AI models used by government departments.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
There is currently no central tracking of use of models within government, but there is a relevant initiative focused on algorithmic transparency and some further planned activity in the Cabinet Office.

For tools that have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interact with the public, government publishes information via the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS). The ATRS captures comprehensive information about algorithmic tools, including about the models they are built on, their design, purpose, governance, and role in decision-making. Publication of records is mandatory for central government and arm's length bodies that deliver front line services, and it is recommended best practice for the wider public sector.

ATRS records are published on GOV.UK. At time of writing, 157 records have been published since the Standard was first launched in 2021. These come from a wide variety of government departments and agencies, with more being added every month. HMG departments are required to identify and produce records for all tools that fall in scope of the ATRS. The Government Digital Service regularly check with departments to ensure that this is on track.

This approach aims to deliver meaningful transparency, where the general public can access high-level explanations quickly and easily, and specialised or interested parties can explore more detailed information as they wish.

The Cabinet Office Future Civil Service team are looking to create a centralised view on AI deployment across departments. The recently established the GovAI Unit within the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, will coordinate, develop and scale AI solutions across Government in collaboration with the Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce. The Government is committed to the ethical and transparent deployment of AI with appropriate guardrails, as our overriding principle.

writtenQuestions.answerText:
Decisions on whether to investigate, enforce, or sanction regulated services are for the independent regulator. The government has been clear that effective enforcement of Online Safety Act duties is a priority. Ministers and officials meet regularly with Ofcom to discuss the implementation and enforcement of the Act.

The Act lists certain fraud offences as ‘priority offences’, meaning regulated services must prevent users encountering user-generated fraudulent content, swiftly remove it if it appears, and manage risks of their services facilitating fraud. Additional duties for Category 1 and 2A services to tackle paid-for fraudulent advertising are expected to be in effect in 2027.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the legal liability of AI agents, particularly in instances of AI hallucination.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the potential for harm where AI systems, including AI agents, produce inaccurate or misleading outputs. Existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to the development and use of AI systems, including AI agents. Whether liability arises in a particular case, including where harm results from an inaccurate or misleading output, will depend on the facts, the applicable law and the responsibilities of the parties involved.

The Government continues to consider how existing frameworks apply as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. Where the evidence shows that changes are necessary to ensure the safety of the British public, we will act.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what estimate she has made of the additional annual administrative and IT costs to the Student Loans Company of operating and auditing student finance systems; and what steps she is taking to ensure that borrowers do not cross-subsidise those administrative overheads.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Student Loans Company (SLC) is a non-profit making executive non-departmental public body. The company is wholly in public ownership and acts on behalf of the four UK governments. As a result, its operating costs come from public funds, meaning UK taxpayers ultimately finance the organisation.

The SLC works closely with the department to ensure taxpayer funding is protected. This is being achieved by further strengthening its approach to identifying and preventing fraud and error.

Each year, the SLC publishes its Annual Report and Accounts, which includes its total operational costs for managing the student loan book, administering loans and grants to students, and paying tuition fees to universities and colleges across the UK. The latest report is available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/slc-annual-report-and-accounts-2025-to-2026/slc-annual-report-and-accounts-2025-2026.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what assessment her Department has made of trends in the level of teacher recruitment and retention challenges in specialist subjects, including modern foreign languages, music and digital skills, ahead of the implementation of the reformed Key Stage 3 curriculum.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department recognises the value of strong teachers working in every classroom across key stage 3 and key stage 4. That is why we have recruited more than 3,000 new secondary teachers, continue to invest in initial teacher training and have set out plans through the Schools White Paper for a Teacher Training Entitlement, so that every teacher can access high-quality professional development.

Our schoolteacher pipeline is also growing, with nearly 32,600 new entrants to Initial Teacher Training (ITT) in Autumn 2025, up 13% from the previous year. There were 17,200 entrants to secondary postgraduate ITT (PGITT) courses in the 2025/26 academic year, 1,900 more than in the 2024/25 academic year.

Modern foreign languages had 1,378 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 1,179 in 2024/25, which is a 17% increase.

Music had 369 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 345 in 2024/25, which is a 7% increase.

Computing had 723 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, a 46% increase on 2024/25. This is the highest number of computing PGITT entrants since comparable statistics began in 2012/13.
writtenQuestions.heading: Teachers: Labour Turnover and Recruitment

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, how her Department plans to measure the impact of the reformed Key Stage 3 curriculum and enrichment framework on reducing persistent school absence among disadvantaged pupils in Leicester East constituency.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Tackling persistent absence is a key priority, especially among disadvantaged pupils. The department’s world-leading attendance data tools allow us to monitor attendance rates and understand the drivers of persistent absence, informing a targeted approach where challenges are greatest.

Our refreshed national curriculum is designed to be broad, engaging and inspire a love of learning. Our new key stage 3 curriculum will provide a distinct and exciting three year programme of study, and schools should no longer begin teaching GCSEs to entire year 9 cohorts.

The department has published the Enrichment Framework, with benchmarks to provide a clear, simple structure against which schools and colleges can evaluate their own provision and make considered improvements to their offer, including consideration of how this can build into wider priorities like attendance. We are continuing to monitor and build the emerging evidence base on the connection between enrichment and attendance.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, pursuant to the Answer of 19 October 2026 to Question 34891, what criteria her Department used to select the schools, academy trusts and local authorities it engaged in developing the proposed Management Information System (MIS) framework; whether participants were recruited by inviting responses from organisations that had experienced difficulties with MIS suppliers; and what steps her Department took to ensure that their views were representative of all schools in England.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Engagement for the Management Information System (MIS) framework project was in line with the department’s approach with getting user research from schools. The schools that have agreed to participate in this research are contacted directly after registering their interest and the research pool is a representative sample from all schools in England. In addition, all schools in England were contacted via the department's update service to advise them of the project and ask if they wanted to participate. Over 50 interviews and discussions took place to inform the development of the framework, with a representative range of education organisations, including single schools, multi-academy trusts (MATs), local authority maintained schools and local authorities.

Some of these participants also formed part of the working group. Participants included headteachers, school business managers, trust finance and procurement leads, technical specialists and MIS users. Engagement covered primary, secondary, special educational needs and disabilities, and other specialist settings schools, together with smaller schools and larger MATs. This ensured that requirements were informed by organisations with different governance models, operational structures, procurement capability and MIS maturity levels.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether participation in the proposed education technology (EdTech) certification scheme will be mandatory or voluntary for suppliers of EdTech products.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, the certification scheme would not initially be mandatory. The department does not currently have specific powers to require suppliers to obtain certification or education settings to use certified products.

The department proposes instead to set a clear expectation through statutory guidance that education settings should obtain proportionate assurance that products within the scheme’s scope meet the relevant safety standards. Certification would ordinarily provide that assurance, while allowing settings to rely on equivalent evidence where this is justified. The consultation also seeks views on whether legislative underpinning may be needed in future.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether the standards assessed by the proposed education technology certification scheme will include (1) children’s physical and mental health implications, (2) data privacy implications, and (3) superiority of learning outcomes.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, products would be assessed against a range of criteria including data privacy, and children’s mental health and cognitive, social and emotional development. The consultation also seeks views on whether there are additional risks that the scheme proposal currently does not cover.

Physical health is not proposed as a separate certification criterion and certification would not assess a product’s overall educational effectiveness, except where a lack of effectiveness could put children at risk of harm.

The department will continue to support settings to make evidence-informed decisions about product effectiveness through guidance and evidence on what works, including the EdTech Testbed programme in partnership with the Education Endowment Foundation.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the impact that devolution of the 16-to-19 skills budget would have on colleges whose student catchment areas are regional or national rather than local.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department will empower strategic authorities to offer locally tailored technical and vocational routes for people aged 16 and over, underpinned by control of the budget for 16 to 19-year-olds.

The purpose of these reforms is to expand opportunity, not restrict it. Strategic authorities can help bring together education, skills, employers, and other services around young people's needs while ensuring provision is better aligned to local opportunities and labour market demand. The department’s ambition is for stronger local leadership and greater consistency in outcomes, not opportunity that varies by postcode.

The detailed design of future devolved arrangements for 16 to 19 technical education remains under development and we will continue to work with strategic authorities and the sector on this.

This includes consideration of strategic authority and provider funding arrangements, and how any future arrangements would operate for different provider types, such as specialist land based colleges and learner cohorts, including where learners access provision beyond their local area.

writtenQuestions.answerText:

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, whether his Department collects data on the employment outcomes of workers made redundant from technology and digital occupations, including (a) the average length of time before securing new employment and (b) changes in earnings following re-employment; and what support his Department provides to such workers who remain unemployed six months after redundancy.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Department for Work and Pensions monitors data published by the independent Office for National Statistics on the estimated number of redundancies by industry. Such industries include ‘Information & communication’ and ‘Professional, Scientific & Technical Activities’. This data may be accessed using this link: RED02: Redundancies by age, industry and region - Office for National Statistics

The Department provides support to employers and individuals affected by redundancy through its Rapid Response Service. The service aims to help people move quickly into alternative employment and can provide tailored support including help with job search and CVs, identifying transferable skills, accessing appropriate training and overcoming barriers to securing new employment. Support can begin when an individual is under threat of redundancy or during their notice period and can normally continue for up to 13 weeks following redundancy, whether or not the individual makes a claim to benefit.

The Department also reviews published data on the duration of Universal Credit (UC) claims, and the rate at which UC customers in the ‘searching for work’ conditionality regime enter employment. This analysis can be accessed using this link: Get Britain Working: Labour Market Insights October 2026 - GOV.UK

The Department for Work and Pensions offers a range of employment support, including the ‘Find a Job’ website, financial support through the Flexible Support Fund to help with interviews or starting work, and tailored, flexible support through Jobcentre Plus. Where appropriate, Work Coaches identify skill gaps and signpost jobseekers to relevant training and provision, such as Skills Bootcamps, apprenticeships, sector-based work academy programmes, and free courses for jobs, as well as essential English, maths and digital skills. For those who have been on Universal Credit for 6 months or more, the Restart Scheme provides 12 months of more intensive support, including bespoke action plans.

The DWP Careers Service in England provides free, impartial careers support through to anyone who is looking for work, who wants to get on in work, or who wants to change their career or retrain, regardless of whether they are claiming benefits. Careers information and advice is available via the digital offer, Get Careers Information and Advice.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, (a) what standards will govern the inclusion or exclusion of detailed psychotherapy and psychological therapy session notes relating to children in the Single Patient Record and (b) what assessment has been made of whether existing shared care records apply equivalent safeguards.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
In respect of the Single Patient Record, discussions are ongoing on a range of practical issues about its scope and operation, and that includes determining what arrangements should apply to the sharing of psychotherapy and psychological therapy records, including the highly personal and private information contained in the notes of therapy sessions.

No final decisions have been made in this area, and we are extremely mindful of the views of patient groups, therapy professionals and other stakeholders, and of the debates that have previously taken place in other contexts about the need to prevent inappropriate third party access to confidential therapy notes. We will provide further updates in due course.

More generally, the controllers of a shared care record are required under the common law duty of confidentiality to communicate adequately to their local communities the existence and purposes of a shared care record, its impact on individuals and their right to object to some or all of their confidential patient information being included within that shared record.

Furthermore, the controllers of the shared care record must also ensure that they comply with UK General Data Protection Regulation requirements that data is processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, making reasonable efforts to ensure that individuals are informed about how their personal data is used.

In accordance with s251B of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, it is appropriate for clinicians to share information through a shared care record with other clinicians responsible for a patient’s care, unless that patient objects, or it is reasonable for them to believe that the patient would object. When it is necessary for direct care purposes, for example in an emergency situation, and those purposes are consistent with the reasonable expectations of the individual patient, health professionals will also rely on an assumption of consent to share essential information with other professionals responsible for the patient’s care.

However, as with all health records, there are strict rules and guidance in place to prevent unauthorised, inappropriate and unjustifiable access to confidential patient information by NHS employees, regardless of whether that information is held on a shared record, with staff who breach those rules facing suspension, dismissal and potential prosecution.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what methodology her Department uses to determine monthly NHS Drug Tariff price concessions; and for what reasons concessionary reimbursement rates for essential medicines, including Flucloxacillin oral solution, were set below wholesale purchase costs in October 2026.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Further to the answer provided on 19 March in response to Question 120781, we have two arrangements in place to reduce community pharmacies dispensing at a loss and to ensure that overall, they are paid enough as part of their Community Pharmacy Contractual Framework funding. These are the medicine margin arrangements and concessionary prices.

The Department assesses the medicine margin, the difference between the reimbursement price and the price the pharmacy was charged by the supplier, through a quarterly medicine margin survey, which ensures that in totality, pharmacies are paid the allowed medicine margin above what it cost them to purchase medicines overall.

Concessionary prices are an in-month increase in the reimbursement price of a product listed in the Drug Tariff, when the market price of a medicine suddenly increases. The Department considers concessionary price requests that come directly from the Community Pharmacy England (CPE) on behalf of community pharmacies.

Concessionary prices are set using ‘real-time’ market data provided to the Department under the Health Service Products (Provision and Disclosure of Information) Regulations 2018 on prices and stock levels intended for retail pharmacy businesses in England. The regulations ensure that all suppliers of a product have to supply data to the Department to underpin the concessionary price setting mechanism. An initial concessionary price is proposed by the Department to CPE, and we then enter negotiations for each individual concessionary price.

Market prices can vary during a month for a number of reasons, and we often see a range of prices available to pharmacy contractors. We continue to work with CPE to ensure that the concessionary price is set to reflect prevailing market prices and availability during the relevant period and are published as soon as possible. In addition, there is a ‘retrospective top-up payment for concessionary prices’, which provides an additional payment to contractors when the margin survey indicates that despite a concessionary price, there was an under payment for a specific product.

No specific assessment has been made in relation to independent community pharmacies in Leicester East and Leicestershire, but on the wider issues raised, I refer the Hon Member to the answers provide on 1 June to Question 3946, and on 21 May to Question 1474.

Finally, further to the answer of 17 June to Question 6747, community pharmacies in England receive an advance payment in accordance with Clause 5C of the Drug Tariff. Where prescriptions are submitted by the relevant deadline, pharmacies typically receive this payment around 11 to 12 days after the end of the dispensing month. The advance payment is intended to support contractor cash flow while final pricing and reconciliation are completed and assist pharmacies in meeting wholesaler bills at the end of the month.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what assessment her Department has made of the impact of NHS Drug Tariff reimbursement on the financial viability and cash flow of independent community pharmacies in Leicester East and Leicestershire.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Further to the answer provided on 19 March in response to Question 120781, we have two arrangements in place to reduce community pharmacies dispensing at a loss and to ensure that overall, they are paid enough as part of their Community Pharmacy Contractual Framework funding. These are the medicine margin arrangements and concessionary prices.

The Department assesses the medicine margin, the difference between the reimbursement price and the price the pharmacy was charged by the supplier, through a quarterly medicine margin survey, which ensures that in totality, pharmacies are paid the allowed medicine margin above what it cost them to purchase medicines overall.

Concessionary prices are an in-month increase in the reimbursement price of a product listed in the Drug Tariff, when the market price of a medicine suddenly increases. The Department considers concessionary price requests that come directly from the Community Pharmacy England (CPE) on behalf of community pharmacies.

Concessionary prices are set using ‘real-time’ market data provided to the Department under the Health Service Products (Provision and Disclosure of Information) Regulations 2018 on prices and stock levels intended for retail pharmacy businesses in England. The regulations ensure that all suppliers of a product have to supply data to the Department to underpin the concessionary price setting mechanism. An initial concessionary price is proposed by the Department to CPE, and we then enter negotiations for each individual concessionary price.

Market prices can vary during a month for a number of reasons, and we often see a range of prices available to pharmacy contractors. We continue to work with CPE to ensure that the concessionary price is set to reflect prevailing market prices and availability during the relevant period and are published as soon as possible. In addition, there is a ‘retrospective top-up payment for concessionary prices’, which provides an additional payment to contractors when the margin survey indicates that despite a concessionary price, there was an under payment for a specific product.

No specific assessment has been made in relation to independent community pharmacies in Leicester East and Leicestershire, but on the wider issues raised, I refer the Hon Member to the answers provide on 1 June to Question 3946, and on 21 May to Question 1474.

Where prescriptions are submitted by the relevant deadline, pharmacies typically receive this payment around 11 to 12 days after the end of the dispensing month. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what steps she is taking to ensure that people with severe and very severe ME/CFS receive care in accordance with NICE guidance.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is committed to improving care and support for people with myalgic encephalomyelitis, also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). We recognise the devastating impact the condition can have on patients and their families, particularly those living with severe and very severe ME/CFS.

The Department published the final ME/CFS delivery plan for England in July 2025. Developed with patients, carers, clinicians, charities, and other partners, the plan sets out actions across three themes: research; attitudes and education; and living with ME/CFS. On 9 October 2026, the Department provided an update to the chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on ME and the stakeholder engagement group on implementation, including on progress made and the challenges remaining.

Integrated care boards (ICBs) are responsible for commissioning ME/CFS services to meet the needs of their local populations. Healthcare professionals are expected to take the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline on ME/CFS fully into account when providing care. The Department and NHS England are developing a template service specification to support commissioners and providers to deliver appropriate, NICE aligned services. Following engagement with clinicians, patient organisations, and people with lived experience, its scope has been expanded from mild and moderate ME/CFS to also include severe ME/CFS. Once completed, it will be circulated to ICBs.

The delivery plan also includes an action to explore whether a specialised service should be prescribed for very severe ME/CFS. This remains under active consideration, taking into account all appropriate clinical, commissioning, and operational advice.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what additional support her Department is providing to local authority adult safeguarding teams to help them manage increased demand during the winter months.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Hon Member raises important issues in his question, which will be under consideration by Baroness Casey, as she develops proposals on the care workforce through her commission on adult social care, including staff responsible for adult safeguarding. The Government has brought Baroness Casey’s final report forward to next summer, and we will set out next steps once that report is received.

The Government recognises the significant pressures that councils are facing, which is why we have made approximately £4.6 billion of additional funding available for adult social care in 2028/29 compared to 2025/26, to support the sector in making improvements. This forms part of the first multi-year settlement in over a decade.

The Department carries out regular exercises to assess the financial pressures facing adult social care. These assessments account for a wide range of pressures, such as inflation and demographic changes. The Department also works closely with local authorities and the adult social care sector to understand the impact of cost and demand pressures.

The 2026/27 to 2028/29 Local Government Finance Settlement confirmed the Government’s plans to simplify adult social care funding to give local government more flexibility, and to redistribute it to where it is needed most. This will enable local authorities to deliver the Government’s priorities for adult social care within a more flexible funding system and give councils greater discretion over how to use funding to respond to local needs.

The Government is working with local authorities and their partners to manage additional pressures over winter, including through support to maintain effective hospital discharge and ensure people receive the right care in the right place. This work supports local authorities to respond to pressures across adult social care. Local authorities are responsible for delivering their statutory adult social care functions, including safeguarding.

The Local Government Association has been awarded a three-year grant from the Department to deliver an annual programme of universal and targeted support to local authorities and their partners. In 2026/27 this will include a package of universal support to support local authorities on safeguarding and workforce retention.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what assessment has been made of the equitable and inclusive improvement of waiting lists to tackle health inequalities in line with Elective Reform Plan goals.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
While no specific assessment has been made, the Elective Reform Plan (ERP) sets out commitments to tackle disparities in access to and waiting time for elective care.

The plan’s measures include publishing waiting list information disaggregated by demographic information, and improving the use of transparent, accessible, and alternative language templates and prioritisation tools.

Since July 2025, NHS England has published monthly waiting list information, broken down by age, sex, ethnicity, and deprivation, enabling national and local National Health Service teams to identify disparities.

Alongside publication, NHS England has worked with providers to improve the submission and quality of demographic data, strengthening the insight available to understand and address inequalities in elective care.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what the average ambulance response time was for Category 2 emergency calls in England in the latest period for which data is available; and what steps her Department is taking to reduce ambulance waiting times for patients suffering serious conditions including heart attacks and strokes.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Average Category 2 ambulance response times are published monthly and can be found at the link below, but these do not include an assessment of the impact of performance on patient outcomes given the number of other variable factors at work:

https://www.england.nhs.uk/statistics/statistical-work-areas/ambulance-quality-indicators/

In October 2025, the Medium Term Planning Framework set out our clear priorities to improve urgent and emergency care performance across England, including the ambition to reduce Category 2 response times to an average of 18 minutes by end of 2028/29.

This is supported by significant capital investment in the ambulance service, including accelerating ambulance station upgrades and associated infrastructure improvements to improve vehicle availability and reduce downtime. A £75 million fleet upgrade has provided new emergency vehicles to every region of England, and is the largest such upgrade in recent years. Modern, well-equipped, reliable ambulances support staff to respond quickly and safely to patients, and the new vehicles are already helping to reduce response times.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what plans she has to improve mental health services.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText: We are investing a record £16.3 billion in National Health Service mental health services this year and recruiting thousands of additional mental health workers to ensure that everyone who needs support is able to access it at the earliest opportunity, and as conveniently as possible. In addition, we have made £343 million of capital funding available to transform how people access mental health support, including rolling out 100 new community-based mental health centres across England, and 59 mental health emergency departments, helping people get support earlier, closer to home, and in the right setting. Additionally, we are accelerating the rollout of mental health support teams in schools and colleges to reach full national coverage by 2029. Our forthcoming Mental Health Strategy will aim to transform mental health care into a system that responds earlier, reduces waiting times for support, intervenes before distress escalates to diagnosis or crisis, and supports people to stay active and participate in education, work, family, and community life.

writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
In January, following national review, NHS England confirmed to integrated care boards (ICBs) the functions which are not core to strategic commissioning and which ICBs should plan to transfer in 2026/27. These functions are:

  • oversight of provider performance under the National Health Service performance assessment framework;

  • local workforce development and training including recruitment and retention;

  • estates and infrastructure strategy; and

  • data collection, management, and processing.

There are no target dates for other functions.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what plans they have, if any, to amend the Care Quality Commission's inspection framework or introduce legislative changes where appropriate, to ensure that cyber resilience is assessed as part of health and social care providers' responsibilities for safe care, operational continuity, governance and the protection of people's information.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is a self-assessment toolkit that must be completed by health and social care providers to access National Health Service data. The DSPT’s requirements include a minimum data security training requirement for staff, organisational policies governing the use of personal devices, and the management of unsupported systems.

To support social care providers in strengthening their cyber security and resilience, the Department established the Better Security, Better Care (BSBC) programme in 2021. The programme provides guidance, training, and a dedicated helpline to help care providers complete the DSPT. The programme works with system partners, including the Care Quality Commission (CQC), to better ensure cyber security is prioritised across the adult social care sector. Alongside this support, care providers can also access the NHS Cyber Alerts service to receive up-to-date intelligence on potential cyber vulnerabilities, enabling them to take appropriate action.

Since the BSBC programme began in March 2021, the Department has invested £23 million in improving cyber resilience across the adult social care sector, with over 21,000 CQC registered care provider locations now completing the DSPT. Funding for the programme will continue until March 2029, supporting the adult social care sector to strengthen its cyber resilience as it progresses towards the Government’s ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ adult social care sector.

NHS England assures 23 digital social care record (DSCR) software solutions against core capabilities and a set of overarching standards. As part of this assurance, suppliers that deliver the assured DSCR solutions are required to meet several cyber security standards, including the DSPT, Cyber Essentials Plus, and ISO 27001. This gives social care providers greater confidence in the security of the digital solutions they use, supporting access to NHS services and enabling better care for people who draw on care and support. In addition to the work on cyber resilience delivery, the ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ sector also includes support to care providers to either migrate from existing legacy systems to assured DSCRs or to ensure that their legacy systems meet assurance requirements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the cyber security risks associated with the widespread use of personal devices by the adult social care workforce; and what steps they are taking to support social care providers in reducing those risks.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is a self-assessment toolkit that must be completed by health and social care providers to access National Health Service data. The DSPT’s requirements include a minimum data security training requirement for staff, organisational policies governing the use of personal devices, and the management of unsupported systems.

To support social care providers in strengthening their cyber security and resilience, the Department established the Better Security, Better Care (BSBC) programme in 2021. The programme provides guidance, training, and a dedicated helpline to help care providers complete the DSPT. The programme works with system partners, including the Care Quality Commission (CQC), to better ensure cyber security is prioritised across the adult social care sector. Alongside this support, care providers can also access the NHS Cyber Alerts service to receive up-to-date intelligence on potential cyber vulnerabilities, enabling them to take appropriate action.

Since the BSBC programme began in March 2021, the Department has invested £23 million in improving cyber resilience across the adult social care sector, with over 21,000 CQC registered care provider locations now completing the DSPT. Funding for the programme will continue until March 2029, supporting the adult social care sector to strengthen its cyber resilience as it progresses towards the Government’s ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ adult social care sector.

NHS England assures 23 digital social care record (DSCR) software solutions against core capabilities and a set of overarching standards. As part of this assurance, suppliers that deliver the assured DSCR solutions are required to meet several cyber security standards, including the DSPT, Cyber Essentials Plus, and ISO 27001. This gives social care providers greater confidence in the security of the digital solutions they use, supporting access to NHS services and enabling better care for people who draw on care and support. In addition to the work on cyber resilience delivery, the ambition for a ‘fully digitised’ sector also includes support to care providers to either migrate from existing legacy systems to assured DSCRs or to ensure that their legacy systems meet assurance requirements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government when they intend to publish the updated national service specification for specialised rheumatology, and what steps they are taking to ensure that revised standards for multidisciplinary care, staffing, and specialist network provision are implemented across integrated care boards for people living with rare autoimmune rheumatic diseases.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
I refer the Noble Lord to the answer provided on 26 October in response to Question 36778, which, for ease of reference, is reproduced below.

“NHS England has published a national service specification relating to specialised rheumatology which includes the management of patients with rare autoimmune rheumatic diseases. The specification is available at the following link:

https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/a13-spec-rheumatology.pdf

This specification is in the process of being refreshed to recognise the current practice of services working through a networked approach to ensure care of patients is addressed in the service most appropriate to their needs.

Commissioning responsibility for specialised rheumatology services has been delegated to integrated care boards, but there continues to be a requirement for services to meet national service specifications and standards.”

In addition, I also refer the Noble Lord to the answer provided on 19 June in response to Question HL779, which, for ease of reference, is reproduced below.

“The Government is committed to improving the lives of those living with rare diseases under the UK Rare Diseases Framework. We published the fifth annual England action plan in February 2026, where we report on the steps we have taken to advance the priorities of the framework.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published a Quality Standard for Rare Diseases in February 2026 covering diagnosing, managing and treating rare diseases in children, young people and adults. NICE Quality Standards are concise statements designed to drive measurable improvements in care, and Integrated Care Boards are expected to take them fully into account in the design of services that meet the needs of their local populations.

Rare autoimmune rheumatic diseases, such as lupus, scleroderma, myositis, Sjögren’s disease and vasculitis, do not each have their own dedicated service specifications. Instead, care for these conditions is delivered through Specialised Rheumatology Services and Specialised Immunology Services, alongside linked services including renal, dermatology, endocrinology, hepatology and neurology. These service specifications set out the core requirements for clinical teams and how they should coordinate patient care. Where a specific care coordinator role is not defined within the specification, clinical nurse specialists often take on this responsibility.

The National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) in NHS England collects, curates, quality assures and analyses data on people with rare and congenital conditions across the whole of England. NDRS continues to develop approaches to improve rare disease case ascertainment through collection and linkage of multiple datasets. For rare autoimmune conditions specifically, NDRS has reported on several of these conditions within the Rare Conditions Registration Statistics and has published several peer-reviewed articles in this area.

NHS England requires data submission to the relevant Specialised Services Quality Dashboard as part of contractual requirements. These often include specific patient experience measures such as quality-of-life scores. In the future, it is expected that the Department will maintain a national framework of standards, service specifications and policies to support services.”

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they are taking to establish clear clinical pathways for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) care and ensure wider, more equitable, and accessible use of COPD biologics in relevant cases.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
I refer the Noble Lord to the answer provided on 22 July in response to Question HL2132, which, for ease of reference, is reproduced below:

The Government recognises that many respiratory diseases are associated with preventable risk factors, including smoking, air pollution, occupational exposures, poor housing conditions, and delayed diagnosis.

Data published by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities shows that the under 75 year old mortality rate from respiratory disease considered preventable in England was 19.6 deaths per 100,000 population in 2024.

The Government is taking action to reduce respiratory disease morbidity and mortality through measures that prevent disease, improve early diagnosis, and support effective treatment, including implementation of the Tobacco and Vapes Act, support for local smoking cessation services, improvements in air quality, vaccination programmes against respiratory infections, and delivery of NHS Long Term Plan commitments on respiratory disease.

NHS England's National Respiratory Programme is focused on improving outcomes for people with respiratory disease through earlier diagnosis, better disease management, and access to effective and innovative treatments. This includes improving access to quality-assured spirometry, pulmonary rehabilitation, and earlier diagnosis of conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), supported by commissioning standards and guidance for commissioners.

NHS England, working with Health Innovation Networks, has also established a multi-year Respiratory Transformation Partnership to identify scalable approaches to reducing premature mortality, improving disease recognition, supporting the consistent delivery of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended care, and increasing access to existing and emerging biologic therapies for people living with asthma and COPD. A nationally coordinated evaluation will support evidence generation, shared learning, and future investment decisions.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, how many hotels were in use as asylum accommodation on the latest date for which data is available; how many people were accommodated in them; what the average daily cost per person was; and by what date she expects the use of hotels to end.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As of the 19 November, there are around 140 hotels in use. This is down from 197 at the start of the year and over 400 at their peak in 2023, with more to close in the months ahead.

The latest figures show that at the end of June 2026 16,021 people were staying in hotels, 50% lower than at the end of June 2025, and 71% lower than the peak of 56,018 at the end of September 2023.

As we close hotels, average daily costs have risen to £199 per person per night as a result of low utilisation. This is a necessary and short-term byproduct of our commitment to close all hotels by the end of this Parliament. We are on track to deliver just that.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what assessment her Department made of the potential merits of including Biomedical Scientists in the 5 year ILR settlement route for NHS healthcare professionals.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, following a 12-week public consultation, the Home Secretary announced the Government's new framework for earned settlement. This new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

Under Earned Settlement, eligible workers in specified health and education occupations (for instance, doctors, nurses and teachers) will be able to qualify for settlement after five years, provided they meet the other settlement requirements. The qualifying occupations will be those health and education public-sector roles that are already identified in the Immigration Rules as being paid according to national pay scales. This follows the independent advice of the Migration Advisory Committee on the treatment of these occupations.

The list of occupations where public sector pay scales apply is subject to review. In its December 2025 review of salary requirements, the MAC suggested the Government may wish to consider adding biomedical scientists to this list. On 28 October 2026 the Chancellor announced that the Government would be accepting the MAC’s recommendations. The Home Office will set out the details of how it intends to implement the Budget announcement on the MAC's salary report ahead of the Immigration Rules change next spring.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, will the Department publish ASRU audit and inspection findings for 2025.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is committed to transparency in the regulation of animals used in science.

The Animals in Science Regulation Unit (ASRU) publishes an annual report providing a public account of its work to assess and enforce compliance with the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986. This includes information on the types and number of audits carried out, as well as summaries of confirmed cases of non-compliance, the nature of the breaches, the number of animals involved, and the regulatory action taken.

The Government is committed to protecting animal welfare through effective regulation and transparency. It is important that our approach to publication supports, rather than undermines, inspectors’ ability to identify and address welfare or compliance risks. The Home Office therefore does not routinely publish individual audit or inspection reports, recognising the importance of full, timely and candid exchanges between inspectors, establishments and staff, including about emerging concerns.

ASRU’s Annual Report for 2025 will be published in due course.
writtenQuestions.heading: Animal Experiments: Inspections

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent steps she has taken to tackle online threats of (a) rape, (b) sexual abuse and (c) intimidation of women and girls through social media platforms.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
This Government recognises that technology can create new opportunities for perpetrators of VAWG, and we are committed to preventing and tackling abuse that occurs online.

In January 2024, the Online Safety Act introduced a threatening communications offence, which criminalised sending communications that threaten death, serious injury, and rape, where the sender intends for the recipient to fear that the threat will be carried out.

The Act requires also requires in-scope platforms, including social media platforms, to proactively tackle harmful and illegal content online. This includes proactively removing content that constitutes harassment, fear or provocation of violence, and sexual exploitation, all of which are priority offences.

The Home Office is investing in a pilot network of covert online officers to improve capabilities in identifying and targeting the most technologically sophisticated VAWG offenders. Insights gained from the pilot will be shared with Ofcom to help address the use of online platforms to cause harm.
writtenQuestions.heading: Gender Based Violence: Social Media

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent steps her Department has taken to tackle (a) online racial discrimination, (b) online religious discrimination and (c) other forms of online hate.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is determined to tackle all forms of hate crime, both online and offline. We have robust legislation in place to deal with threatening, abusive or harassing behaviour and the stirring up of racial and religious hatred. This includes communications offences under the Malicious Communications Act 1988 and Communications Act 2003, and the false and threatening communications offences in the Online Safety Act 2023.

Hate crime is also designated as a priority offence under the Online Safety Act 2023. Online services must take proactive steps to prevent their services being used to facilitate or commit such offences and have systems and processes in place to tackle illegal content.

The Government has increased funding to the police National Online Hate Crime Hub, providing £1.6 million per year to increase and improve the investigative capability of the police to tackle online hate. It also funds True Vision, which enables victims to report hate crime online.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent assessment she has made of the adequacy of the Unsafe Journey Policy; and whether she has made an assessment of the potential merits of waiving biometric requirements for families in Gaza.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Biometric enrolment (in the form of facial images and fingerprints) underpins identity assurance, national and border security, and the integrity of the immigration system. It enables checks against immigration and criminality records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls. It also supports safeguarding, particularly of children, by helping to verify applicants’ identities and reduce the risk of identity fraud and exploitation.

Given the strong public interest in biometric checks, deferring or excusing enrolment before arrival in the UK must remain an exceptional step.

The Government keeps all of its policies, including the Unsafe Journeys Policy, under review. This ensures that it appropriately balances the circumstances of vulnerable applicants with the need to secure the UK borders and maintain effective immigration control. The Unsafe Journeys policy was last updated in March 2026.

The Government recognises the exceptionally difficult circumstances facing families in Gaza. Requests for biometric deferral and excusal are considered on a case-by-case basis, taking account of individual circumstances and relevant human rights obligations.

The existing policy provides a mechanism for considering exceptional circumstances while maintaining these essential safeguards.
writtenQuestions.heading: Visas: Gaza

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, if she will take steps to ensure that NHS finance assistants, finance officers, accountants, management accountants, finance analysts and finance managers are included in the transitional protections under the Migration Advisory Committee.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, the Home Secretary announced the Government's new framework for earned settlement, following a 12-week public consultation which received more than 200,000 responses. The new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

Targeted transitional arrangements will apply to specified care workers and eligible public-sector workers in health and education who were already in the UK before the publication of the Immigration White Paper in May 2025. These are one-off arrangements for clearly defined existing cohorts and do not provide a wider exemption for everyone already in the UK.

Further information on the transitional arrangements is set out in Chapter 8 of the Government's response to the consultation, available here: A Fairer Pathway to Settlement: Government response to the consultation.

Further guidance will also be published setting out additional technical and operational detail ahead of implementation, informed by continued engagement with affected groups and stakeholders.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what transitional protection, if any, will apply to the eligible dependants of people progressing towards settlement under the five-year route.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, the Home Secretary announced the Government's new framework for earned settlement, following a 12-week public consultation which received more than 200,000 responses. The new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

The Government has introduced targeted transitional arrangements for a small number of clearly defined cohorts who were already in the UK before publication of the Immigration White Paper in May 2025.

Under Earned Settlement, a dependant partner who arrives in the UK at the same time as the principal applicant will be able to settle at the same time, provided they meet the relevant requirements. A partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before settling.

Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents and will not be required to meet the adult contribution requirements. Young adults aged 18 to 24 who retain child dependant status will continue to be able to settle alongside their family. They will be expected to meet the adult mandatory requirements but will not need to meet the individual earnings requirement.

Fees for immigration and nationality applications play an essential role in supporting the sustainable funding of the migration and borders system. It is the Government's policy that those who use and benefit most from the immigration system should contribute towards the cost of operating it, reducing the amount of taxpayer funding required.

Further guidance will also be published setting out additional technical and operational detail ahead of implementation, informed by continued engagement with affected groups and stakeholders.
writtenQuestions.heading: Immigration: Dependants

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what steps she is taking to address the difference between National Living Wage and the Home Office salary threshold set for Indefinite Leave to Remain applicants.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, the Home Secretary announced the Government's new framework for earned settlement, following a 12-week public consultation which received more than 200,000 responses. The new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

The Government believes settlement should recognise sustained contribution to the UK. Those seeking settlement will need to demonstrate a minimum level of economic contribution. This has been aligned to the basic rate of income tax, £12,571 a year. Those making a greater contribution may qualify sooner.

We have listened to concerns that salary alone does not capture every form of contribution. The final framework will therefore recognise contribution through earnings, exceptional talent, qualifying public service and family contribution. Those with a specified British connection will only need to meet the minimum income threshold.

This ensures that permanent settlement reflects sustained economic participation, while setting the minimum threshold at a level that remains achievable for people working part-time or in lower-paid employment.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what safeguards will protect workers approaching five years of qualifying residence when their employer's sponsor licence is revoked through no fault of their own, under the proposed five-year transitional settlement arrangements, particularly where employer failures prevent them from meeting sponsorship or salary requirements.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On 2 November 2026, the Home Secretary announced the Government's new framework for earned settlement, following a 12-week public consultation which received more than 200,000 responses. The new framework will ensure that the time it takes to qualify for settlement reflects an individual's character, contribution, integration and residence.

Those who do not meet the requirements of their care work visa will not qualify after five years.

There is, however, a case for giving those who do not qualify after five years a further opportunity to meet the requirements. The care sector saw exceptional levels of sponsor failure, exploitation and poor practice during the period in which this cohort was recruited. Some workers who came to the UK were left without the work they had been promised, making it harder for them to meet the requirements of the route.

We will therefore give these individuals a second opportunity to meet those requirements. Those who do not qualify for settlement after five years will be able to apply for a further five-year Health and Care visa, restricted to genuine work in the sector. This will give them additional time to meet the requirements before applying for settlement again. They will continue to have no recourse to public funds while on that further visa.

Before implementation, the Government will publish further guidance setting out additional technical and operational detail, informed by continued engagement with affected groups and stakeholders.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what steps her Department has taken to keep under review the potential impact of section 157 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 on people who wear masks for health reasons.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The College of Policing issues guidance to police forces on the use of a broad range of public order powers, including the measures in the Crime and Policing Act 2026 which came into force at the end of June.

The police have a duty to act compatibly with human rights when exercising their powers, and duties and to use their powers proportionately. This includes consideration of the use of masks for medical reasons.

The use of police powers to maintain public order and public safety are operational decisions for the police and dependent on police assessments of the circumstances of each particular incident.

The Government keeps all public order legislation under review to ensure it remains viable and proportionate.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what steps they have taken since identifying the Muslim Brotherhood as a potential source of extremism to establish the extent of its influence in charities, schools, mosques and public institutions in the United Kingdom; and what assessment they have made of the effectiveness of existing safeguards.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government does not comment on specific individuals or groups.

As the extremism landscape is constantly evolving, the Home Office continually seeks to build and refresh its knowledge of the threat it poses. If a group or individual is acting in the extremist space, action will be taken. This includes disrupting the activities of those who seek to radicalise others but operate – often intentionally – below legal thresholds. Where the actions of individuals or groups cross legal thresholds, we will act to prevent harm and safeguard susceptible individuals.

We use the full breadth of Government tools and levers to safeguard vulnerable individuals against content and materials used to radicalise others into terrorism. We keep these safeguards under review and work across government to ensure they remain fit for purpose.
writtenQuestions.heading: Muslim Brotherhood: Radicalism

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government, in light of the Home Office consultation response A Fairer Pathway to Settlement, published on 2 November, what definition of criminal record they intend to apply to the mandatory refusal ground in the forthcoming Immigration Statement of Changes, whether they intend to include non-recordable offences, simple cautions, and convictions for summary-only, non-imprisonable offences; and what assessment they have made of the number of settlement applicants whose sole criminal history falls within those categories.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Where a person has been convicted in the UK for an offence committed when they were aged 18 or above, their application for settlement will be refused. This includes where a person has received a custodial or non-custodial sentence, a community order, a conditional caution, an absolute or conditional discharge or a fine. It does not include simple cautions.

No assessment has been made of the number of settlement applicants who will be affected by this change.
writtenQuestions.heading: Migrants: Offenders

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether, and if so how, future arrangements for people in the UK under the Ukraine schemes will provide long-term permission to remain for people with lifelong disabilities; and for the family members who provide their essential care.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government has always been clear that the Ukraine Schemes offer temporary sanctuary while the conflict continues and do not provide a route to settlement. Time spent in the UK under the Ukraine Schemes also does not count towards the Long Residence route.

The Government is actively considering the longer-term position of Ukrainians in the UK, including the circumstances of those who may face particular barriers to returning to Ukraine, such as people with disabilities and their family members who provide essential care.

The Home Office does not hold recorded data on the number of disabled Ukrainians under the Ukraine Schemes. This work draws on evidence from across government, academia, civil society and stakeholder engagement, including research by the University of Warwick on supporting Ukrainian refugees with disabilities in the UK.

No decisions have yet been taken on future arrangements. We will set out our position to Parliament and the public in due course.
writtenQuestions.heading: Refugees: Ukraine

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what estimate they have made of the annual cost of rural crime to agricultural businesses in England; and how those costs have changed since 2020.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Home Office does not hold data on the annual cost of rural crime to agricultural businesses in England. Rural crime is not recorded as a separate category in national crime statistics. Offences such as theft, criminal damage and wildlife crime are recorded within existing crime categories instead.

The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) Mutual publish annual reports on the cost of rural crime which rose to a peak in 2023 before falling in 2024 and 2025.

Reports provided UK-wide estimates of £43.3 million for 2020, £40.5 million for 2021, £49.5 million for 2022 (subsequently reported as £50.6 million), £52.8 million for 2023, £44.1 million for 2024 and £41.5 million for 2025. These industry estimates are based on NFU Mutual’s insurance claims data, are subject to revision and are not Government estimates of the cost of rural crime to agricultural businesses in England.
writtenQuestions.heading: Agriculture: Crime

writtenQuestions.answerText: Data on job titles explicitly including social media for all civil servants is not held centrally and could only be provided at a disproportionate cost. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what steps he is taking to ensure that the armed forces are prepared for any attack on a NATO country.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The UK’s commitment to NATO is unwavering. NATO is a defensive Alliance: we do not seek conflict, but we are clear that we will defend every inch of Allied territory. Our NATO-first approach puts the Alliance at the heart of how we organise, equip and train our Armed Forces, driving improvements in warfighting readiness and ensuring the UK can play its full part in defending the Alliance. That commitment is backed by forces on the ground today, including through our leadership of NATO’s Forward Land Forces in Estonia, alongside our wider land, air and maritime contributions across the Alliance.

We are sustaining this readiness through an ambitious programme of training and exercising with NATO across all domains, from the North Atlantic and High North to NATO’s eastern flank. Our forces train routinely with Allies to strengthen interoperability and practise their ability to reinforce, deploy, integrate and sustain combat power in crisis and conflict. In 2027, the UK will make a major contribution to STEADFAST DEFENDER, NATO’s principal live collective defence exercise. UK-led exercises and activity across multiple domains will test our ability to reinforce Allies, project forces across Europe and sustain combat power at scale as part of NATO’s warfighting plans.

We are backing this with nearly £300 billion of investment in our Armed Forces over the next four years through the Defence Investment Plan, including £15 billion in additional spending power. NATO is at the heart of the Plan, ensuring our investment prioritises the forces and capabilities needed to strengthen UK warfighting readiness and deliver the Alliance’s warfighting plans.
writtenQuestions.heading: Armed Forces

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what assessment has been made of the UK's resilience to grey-zone activity conducted by hostile states.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText: The Government keeps the UK's resilience to hostile state activity under continual review through the National Security Risk Assessment process. Defence works closely with the Cabinet Office and other departments to assess evolving threats, including cyber attacks, sabotage, espionage and disinformation, and to strengthen national resilience in response. This includes testing preparedness through major national and NATO exercises, including the Government's Tier 1 exercise in 2027, ALBISTON SHADOW, which will exercise government responses to hybrid attacks against the UK.
writtenQuestions.heading: Hybrid Warfare

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what assessment he has made of the potential impact of Project Bromo, including the potential locating of Airbus’s Space Systems and Space Digital businesses as the UK component, on the level of UK jobs in the military satellite industry.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government is assessing Project BROMO across relevant Departments, including its potential implications for the UK's space industrial base, national security, sovereign capabilities, critical skills, supply chains and employment.

The final structure and UK footprint of the proposed joint venture have not yet been determined, and it would therefore be premature to quantify its eventual impact on UK employment. The joint venture presents both opportunities and risks for the UK space sector, including the future location of high-value activities, skills, design authority and manufacturing capability.

The Ministry of Defence is working with Departments across Government to ensure that UK defence and national security interests are properly protected, and we will continue to engage with the companies concerned as the proposed joint venture develops.

The Government remains committed to supporting a strong, competitive and resilient UK space sector, capable of sustaining the sovereign capabilities and highly skilled employment needed for our national security and economic growth.
writtenQuestions.heading: Defence: Satellites
