writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, pursuant to the answer of 10 June 2026 to Question 5953 on Travellers: Caravan Sites, whether the pro-development changes in the National Planning Policy Framework are a positive material consideration when considering an application to (a) regularise and (b) authorise an unauthorised traveller site.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government published a new National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) on 17 August 2026. The Framework should be read as a whole, it must be taken into account in preparing the development plan, and it is a material consideration in planning decisions.

Policies relating to traveller sites have been incorporated throughout relevant chapters of the new NPPF to reduce duplication, support equitable outcomes, and provide greater clarity on how traveller sites should be planned for and delivered.

We intend to publish updated planning practice guidance to support the new NPPF and will do so in a phased manner.

Policy HO7 of the new NPPF makes clear that in applying the policies in this Framework, substantial weight should be given to the benefits of providing homes which will contribute towards meeting the evidenced accommodation needs of the community, as identified through needs assessments prepared for the area of the local planning authority and other relevant evidence. This includes, but is not limited to, homes needed for different groups assessed under policy HO1.

In relation to guidance on human rights and equality considerations, I refer the Rt Hon. Member to the answer given to Question UIN 119662 on 18 March 2026. The Planning Inspectorate ensures Inspectors are up to date with legislation, policy, and relevant court judgments, including in relation to human rights and the public sector equality duty.

In relation to Green Belt policy, I refer the Rt Hon. Member to the answer given to Question UIN 12150 on 30 June 2026. The reasons for exempting traveller sites from the Golden Rules are set out in the government response to the 2024 NPPF consultation, which can be found on gov.uk here.

Traveller site applications remain subject to the same policies on environmental impacts, flooding, transport, and environmental quality as other forms of development.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the consultation outcome, Home buying and selling reform roadmap, updated 19 June 2026, how will the property condition report differ from the home condition report previously required under home information packs.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
This government recognises that previous attempts to reform the home buying and selling process did not succeed.

Home Information Packs were criticised for adding cost, relying on jargon and failing to give buyers the information they needed. They were paper-based and introduced without sufficient industry collaboration.

Our approach has been co-developed with industry and will be phased in gradually, building on work to digitalise the home moving process. Sales packs will include property searches and a property condition report, giving buyers important information before they make an offer. The information underpinning sales packs will come from trusted data sources, with clear standards and the ability to update as needed.

We will work with industry to agree the final detail of what should be included in sales packs ahead of legislation.
writtenQuestions.heading: Housing: Sales

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, if she will make it her policy to ban foreign nationals who enter the country through unlawful means to later accessing social housing if they are given leave to remain.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Eligibility for social housing is tightly controlled. If a person’s visa means that they cannot access state benefits or local authority housing assistance, they are not eligible for an allocation of social housing. Migrants arriving in the UK on student or work visas are not eligible and nor are those who arrive in the country illegally with no leave to remain.

When applying for permission to enter or stay in the UK, most migrants must demonstrate that they can financially support themselves and their dependants. For this reason, the majority of temporary migrants are granted permission subject to a No Recourse to Public Funds condition. If a person's immigration status does not allow them recourse to public funds they are not eligible for an allocation of social housing.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to her Department's policy paper entitled Creating a clear, rules-based planning system, published on 17 August 2026, whether her Department plans to place fast food outlets into their own use class; and whether her Department plans to sub-divide Class E.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Hot food takeaways are classed as sui generis in the Use Classes Order. They are defined as premises where the primary purpose is the sale of hot food where consumption of that food is mostly undertaken off the premises.

The replacement of the previous A5 hot food takeaway use class with sui generis allows local planning authorities to have greater control, through using the planning application process, to prevent the proliferation of hot food takeaways. It is for local planning authorities to determine the use of individual premises and to apply planning policy in the circumstances of each case.

I otherwise refer the hon. Member to the government response to Question 161 of the proposed reforms to the NPPF and other changes to the planning system consultation, which can be found on gov.uk here. We will set out next steps in due course.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what steps are being taken to ensure that a) all developers become active participants in the NHOS and New Homes Quality Code schemes, and b) to ensure that all new homes are covered by the the NHOS and New Homes Quality Code.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government has not announced a timeline but remains committed, in consultation with the Scottish and Welsh Governments, to implementing a statutory UK-wide New Homes Ombudsman scheme and developing and approving a single mandatory consumer code for all housebuilders operating in the UK.

In the interim, we remain supportive of the voluntary New Homes Ombudsman Service and New Homes Quality Code for registered developers.

New build homes are normally issued with a 10-year warranty and as a condition of obtaining a warranty, developers will have to comply with the requirements of the relevant consumer code or the voluntary New Homes Ombudsman Service if they are registered with it.

The Office for National Statistics publishes annual housing affordability ratios for national and subnational geographies in England and Wales, calculated as the ratio of house prices to gross annual earnings, which can be found on their website here. My Department does not currently collect data on the time taken between the granting of planning permission for a residential development and its completion; the number of homes for which planning permission has expired without development commencing; or the numbers of homes with planning permission where development is delayed (or the reason for any such delay).

In May 2025, we published a Planning Reform Working Paper: Speeding Up Build Out inviting views on further action the government should take to speed up homes being built. It can be found on gov.uk here.

On the same day, we launched a technical consultation on implementing measures to improve the transparency of build rates from new residential developments, which includes proposals to implement provisions in Section 113 of the LURA on the power to decline to determine applications. That consultation can be found on gov.uk here.

Utilising the responses received to both consultations, we are progressing a package of build out transparency and accountability measures, including the introduction of commencement notices and development progress reports. This build out data will be incorporated into the new planning application data standard, as part of our plans to digitalise the planning system. We will set out further detail in due course.

I also refer the hon. Member to policy HO13 of the new National Planning Policy Framework published on 17 August 2026.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what assessment she has made of the potential merits of allowing local authorities to give greater priority for social housing to British citizens with a long standing connection to the local area.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Local authorities are responsible for designing and managing their own housing allocations policies to meet local need, including managing their own housing registers (waiting lists).

Local councils already have necessary powers to give priority to local residents, and most are doing so. As of March 2023, 89% of councils had a local connection test and/or a residency test in place.

The government has launched a review into how effectively social housing providers use their properties, including exploring ways to reduce the time homes are left empty, encourage greater movement within the sector to address under-occupancy and overcrowding, and support people to move into more suitable properties.

The government published a response to the previous government’s consultation on reforms to social housing allocations on 2 September 2024. It can be found on gov.uk here.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of changes to national planning guidance on the ability of local authorities to take account of local circumstances when determining planning applications relating to unauthorised encampments.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government published a new National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) on 17 August 2026. The Framework should be read as a whole, it must be taken into account in preparing the development plan, and it is a material consideration in planning decisions.

Policies relating to traveller sites have been incorporated throughout relevant chapters of the new NPPF to reduce duplication, support equitable outcomes, and provide greater clarity on how traveller sites should be planned for and delivered.

We intend to publish updated planning practice guidance to support the new NPPF and will do so in a phased manner.

Policy HO7 of the new NPPF makes clear that in applying the policies in this Framework, substantial weight should be given to the benefits of providing homes which will contribute towards meeting the evidenced accommodation needs of the community, as identified through needs assessments prepared for the area of the local planning authority and other relevant evidence. This includes, but is not limited to, homes needed for different groups assessed under policy HO1.

In relation to guidance on human rights and equality considerations, I refer the Rt Hon. Member to the answer given to Question UIN 119662 on 18 March 2026. The Planning Inspectorate ensures Inspectors are up to date with legislation, policy, and relevant court judgments, including in relation to human rights and the public sector equality duty.

In relation to Green Belt policy, I refer the Rt Hon. Member to the answer given to Question UIN 12150 on 30 June 2026. The reasons for exempting traveller sites from the Golden Rules are set out in the government response to the 2024 NPPF consultation, which can be found on gov.uk here.

Traveller site applications remain subject to the same policies on environmental impacts, flooding, transport, and environmental quality as other forms of development.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the Government response to the proposed reforms to the National Planning Policy Framework and other changes to the planning system consultation, August 2026, page 76, what is the legislative or policy mechanism by which she intends to ban fracking, in addition to the existing moratorium.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
While policy M5 of the new National Planning Policy Framework published on 17 August 2026 introduces a more restrictive approach to proposals for hydrocarbon development, removing the requirement to give great weight to the benefits of onshore oil and gas production, it does not in itself create a statutory prohibition on hydraulic fracturing.

Government policy in other areas maintains that high-volume hydraulic fracturing for shale gas extraction should not take place in England.

The effective moratorium, first introduced via Written Ministerial Statement HCWS68 in 2019 and reinforced in 2022, is being strengthened through provisions contained in the Energy Independence Bill.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the Government response to the proposed reforms to the National Planning Policy Framework and other changes to the planning system consultation, August 2026, page 109, what is the timetable for the review of the Use Classes Order in relation to fast food outlets, and what steps are being taken to prevent the off-sale of heated food from sandwich shops resulting in the premises being classified as hot food takeaways by local planning authorities under the Framework.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Hot food takeaways are classed as sui generis in the Use Classes Order. They are defined as premises where the primary purpose is the sale of hot food where consumption of that food is mostly undertaken off the premises.

The replacement of the previous A5 hot food takeaway use class with sui generis allows local planning authorities to have greater control, through using the planning application process, to prevent the proliferation of hot food takeaways. It is for local planning authorities to determine the use of individual premises and to apply planning policy in the circumstances of each case.

I otherwise refer the hon. Member to the government response to Question 161 of the proposed reforms to the NPPF and other changes to the planning system consultation, which can be found on gov.uk here. We will set out next steps in due course.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what consideration she has given to measures to ensure that a housebuilder's failure to complete agreed infrastructure on existing developments can be taken into account when that housebuilder brings forward proposals for further development in the same local authority area.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Local planning authorities already have a wide range of enforcement powers, with strong penalties for non-compliance.

Where a local planning authority thinks that a condition imposed on a planning permission has not been met, they can serve a breach of condition notice which requires the recipient to remedy the breach within a specified time. There is no appeal against such a notice and failure to comply with it is an offence punishable by an unlimited fine.

An enforcement notice can be served against any breach of planning control – where there is no planning permission for development or the terms of a permission (including a condition) have been breached.

In May 2025, we published a Planning Reform Working Paper: Speeding Up Build Out inviting views on further action the government should take to speed up homes being built. It can be found on gov.uk here.

That consultation can be found on gov.uk here.

Utilising the responses received to both consultations, we are progressing a package of build out transparency and accountability measures and will set out our next steps in due course.

I also refer the hon. Member to policy HO13 of the new National Planning Policy Framework published on 17 August 2026.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the press release entitled Stronger protections and greater confidence for renters, published on 9 September 2026, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of the national landlord registration service on the number of landlords operating in the private rented sector.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Renters’ Rights Act 2025 Impact Assessment can be found on gov.uk here. No separate impact assessment was produced for the Private Rented Sector Database Regulations 2026 because the direct cost impact is below the mandatory assessment threshold. A full impact assessment will be prepared ahead of the second stage of implementation.

The annual service fee for the Private Rented Sector Database is £65 per property. This fee is not subject to VAT. Fees will be pro-rated during the initial roll-out of the ‘Register your rental property’ service to ensure that costs remain fair and that those registering first are not paying more.

The fee will support the cost of operating the service and will ensure councils have the staff and skills required to identify and tackle non-compliance and drive landlords who persist in breaking the law out of the sector.

Where an entire building is comprised of privately rented units, these are classified as individual dwellings and are therefore required to be separately registered with the service. In the case of HMOs, individual rooms do not need to be registered.

We are already exploring how we can make it easier for landlords, particularly those managing large portfolios, to connect their existing property management systems directly with the service to reduce the need to enter the information manually to register properties. We will continue to explore opportunities to improve functionality and reduce burdens as the service develops.

Landlords will be legally required to register all of their properties in England on the service. Local authorities will be able to pursue enforcement activity where landlords are not compliant with this, which includes the power to issue civil penalties. We expect that registration rates will increase over time in line with enforcement of this requirement.

Local councils can begin enforcement action against landlords the day after that region’s registration deadline. During the rollout of the service, if a property is under let and the landlord has failed to register, the landlord may receive a fine of up to £7,000 for an initial breach. For a repeated breach, or for the offence of knowingly or recklessly providing false or misleading information, landlords may be prosecuted or receive a fine of up to £40,000.

My Department is closely monitoring the impact of the Renters’ Rights Act through a comprehensive evaluation programme. We have committed to publish findings two years after implementation in May 2028, and again five years after implementation in May 2031, to assess how the reforms are working for tenants, landlords and the wider private rented sector.

I otherwise refer the hon. Member to the Explanatory Memorandum to the Private Rented Sector Database Regulations 2026 which can be found here.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the press release entitled Stronger protections and greater confidence for renters, published on 9 September 2026, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of the landlord registration service on rents paid by private tenants.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Renters’ Rights Act 2025 Impact Assessment can be found on gov.uk here. No separate impact assessment was produced for the Private Rented Sector Database Regulations 2026 because the direct cost impact is below the mandatory assessment threshold. A full impact assessment will be prepared ahead of the second stage of implementation.

The annual service fee for the Private Rented Sector Database is £65 per property. This fee is not subject to VAT. Fees will be pro-rated during the initial roll-out of the ‘Register your rental property’ service to ensure that costs remain fair and that those registering first are not paying more.

The fee will support the cost of operating the service and will ensure councils have the staff and skills required to identify and tackle non-compliance and drive landlords who persist in breaking the law out of the sector.

Where an entire building is comprised of privately rented units, these are classified as individual dwellings and are therefore required to be separately registered with the service. In the case of HMOs, individual rooms do not need to be registered.

We are already exploring how we can make it easier for landlords, particularly those managing large portfolios, to connect their existing property management systems directly with the service to reduce the need to enter the information manually to register properties. We will continue to explore opportunities to improve functionality and reduce burdens as the service develops.

Landlords will be legally required to register all of their properties in England on the service. Local authorities will be able to pursue enforcement activity where landlords are not compliant with this, which includes the power to issue civil penalties. We expect that registration rates will increase over time in line with enforcement of this requirement.

Local councils can begin enforcement action against landlords the day after that region’s registration deadline. During the rollout of the service, if a property is under let and the landlord has failed to register, the landlord may receive a fine of up to £7,000 for an initial breach. For a repeated breach, or for the offence of knowingly or recklessly providing false or misleading information, landlords may be prosecuted or receive a fine of up to £40,000.

My Department is closely monitoring the impact of the Renters’ Rights Act through a comprehensive evaluation programme. We have committed to publish findings two years after implementation in May 2028, and again five years after implementation in May 2031, to assess how the reforms are working for tenants, landlords and the wider private rented sector.

I otherwise refer the hon. Member to the Explanatory Memorandum to the Private Rented Sector Database Regulations 2026 which can be found here.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, whether her Department has assessed the potential merits of reviewing Section 108 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to create a financial indemnity mechanism or safe-harbour framework for local planning authorities that enact immediate Article 4 Directions to protect local residential character.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
My Department has made no specific assessment of the financial liability incurred by local planning authorities under Section 108 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 when issuing immediate Article 4 Directions to restrict Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs).

Article 39 of the Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015, which can be found on gov.uk here, specifies the contents of an application for a lawful development certificate and how it must be submitted. Further guidance is available in the “lawful development certificates” planning practice guidance, which can be found on gov.uk here.

My Department has published no specific guidance on preventing speculative property conversions from Class C3 to Class C4 during the standard 12-month notification period of a non-immediate Article 4 direction.

My Department has made no assessment of the potential merits of reviewing Section 108 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 and does not collect data on the number of Class C3 to Class C4 small HMO conversions.

The government continues to keep the powers to regulate HMOs under review.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what assessment her Department has made of the potential impact of statutory exemptions from HMO licensing requirements for properties managed by accommodation providers under Home Office Asylum Accommodation and Support Services Contracts on a) on local community cohesion and b) on local planning authority oversight in areas subject to an Article 4 Direction; and whether she plans to ensure all asylum accommodation HMOs comply with local authority mandatory and additional licensing health and safety standards.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
In accordance with the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, the Home Office has a statutory obligation to provide destitute asylum seekers with accommodation and subsistence support while their applications for asylum are being considered. Accommodation is provided on a no-choice basis.

Asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected are generally not provided with dispersal accommodation.

The Home Office consults with local authorities across the UK before dispersal accommodation, including Houses of Multiple Occupation, is procured, ensuring the impact on communities is understood. When considering how much dispersed accommodation to procure in any given area, a range of factors are considered including the local housing availability as well as social factors such as pressures on GPs.

The Housing Act 2004 requires mandatory licensing of HMOs in which five or more people from two or more households share facilities. The 2004 Act also gives local authorities discretion to extend licensing to smaller HMOs in which three or four people from two or more households share facilities. This is known as additional HMO licensing.

All HMOs, regardless of whether they require a licence, must comply with the HMO management regulations. The management regulations set out a number of duties for the landlord and tenant regarding the property, such as taking fire safety measures and providing bins.

Asylum accommodation is within the scope of both HMO management regulations and, where applicable, HMO licensing.

In 2023, the previous government laid regulations to exempt asylum accommodation from HMO licensing. A judicial review was brought against the Statutory Instrument in question and it was subsequently withdrawn in February 2024.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the Answer of 21 January 2025 to Question 21628 on Local Government Finance, and further to Homes England's guidance entitled Council Housebuilding Support Fund: Assessment criteria, updated on 18 September 2026, for what reason the Council Housebuilding Support Fund operates on a bidding basis.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Council Housebuilding Support Fund operates on a competitive bidding basis to ensure public funding is directed towards proposals that best support council-led delivery of social and affordable housing.

The fund supports specific early-stage housing development activity intended to help councils bring forward bids to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme. Councils who intend to bid into this programme are invited to submit proposals setting out the development funding required, how it will be used and the expected delivery timescales.

Applications are assessed against published criteria, including value for money, deliverability and strategic fit. Homes England supports the Department's assessment process by identifying the bids that best meet these criteria and recommending proposals for funding.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, how many planning applications for data centres were (a) received and (b) determined within each AI Growth Zone local planning authority in each year since 2023; and what the median determination time was.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Of the five locations announced as AI growth zones by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, three are in Scotland or Wales where planning is a devolved matter.

My Department does not hold data on the number of data centre applications awaiting permission by local planning authorities (LPAs) under the Town and Country Planning Act. The information in question is held by the individual LPAs.

To date, four requests have been made to direct data centre applications into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects regime under section 35 of the 2008 Planning Act. One was subsequently withdrawn. Three were considered by the Secretary of State and the requests were granted in each case. None of these proposals have been returned for decision following examination by the Planning Inspectorate.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, if she will consider amending the National Scheme of Delegation of Planning Functions to enable an application for a house in multiple occupation that would otherwise fall within Schedule 1 to be considered for referral to a planning committee where it raises significant local planning issues, including the cumulative concentration of HMOs or the loss of family housing.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Whether a particular type of planning application involving HMOs falls within Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 of the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026 will depend on the details of the application and is a matter for the local planning authority concerned.

The government has no plans to amend the national scheme of delegation.

A statutory review clause is included in The Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026 that requires the Secretary of State to publish a review of the operation of the Instrument by 31 October 2028.

Relevant guidance for local planning authorities in England can be found on gov.uk here.

My Department has no plans to issue specific guidance on the treatment of HMOs but we will continue to keep guidance under review.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, whether her Department plans to expand Housing Health and Safety Systems to account for the circumstances of the current occupant.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
A Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS) assessment does not consider the current occupant. It instead takes into account the likelihood of harm for a notional occupant in the most vulnerable age group for a particular hazard.

The only exception to this is the assessment of 'overcrowding and lack of living space' which determines whether a home is suitable for a specific household.

The government has no plans to change the basis on which HHSRS assessments operate.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what assessment her Department has made of the adequacy of the redress available to new-build homeowners where inaccurate information about ongoing estate management charges was provided during the sale of their property.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
It is important that potential buyers have the information they need to make informed decisions about a property. This includes information about estate management charges and responsibility for communal infrastructure.

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 prohibits unfair commercial practices, including misleading actions and misleading omissions. A developer who provides materially inaccurate information or omits material information in circumstances meeting the statutory tests, may therefore breach the Act.

As set out in the Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap published on 19 June 2026, which can be found on gov.uk here, we will publish guidance setting out what information is likely to be “material” to help professionals meet their legal responsibilities under the Act.

I otherwise refer the hon. Members to the Written Ministerial Statement made on 18 December 2025 (HCWS1210). We are currently analysing the feedback received to both consultations referenced in it and will publish our response in due course.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, whether her Department has considered introducing additional protections for purchasers of new-build homes where information provided by a developer on anticipated estate management charges at the point of sale is subsequently found to have been materially inaccurate.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
It is important that potential buyers have the information they need to make informed decisions about a property. This includes information about estate management charges and responsibility for communal infrastructure.

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 prohibits unfair commercial practices, including misleading actions and misleading omissions. A developer who provides materially inaccurate information or omits material information in circumstances meeting the statutory tests, may therefore breach the Act.

As set out in the Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap published on 19 June 2026, which can be found on gov.uk here, we will publish guidance setting out what information is likely to be “material” to help professionals meet their legal responsibilities under the Act.

I otherwise refer the hon. Members to the Written Ministerial Statement made on 18 December 2025 (HCWS1210). We are currently analysing the feedback received to both consultations referenced in it and will publish our response in due course.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, how many social housing properties have been disposed of by registered providers in England in each of the last five years; how many of those properties have ceased to be available for social rent; and what assessment she has made of the potential impact of such disposals on the net supply of social housing in rural areas.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Sales and demolitions are the two main disposals of social housing. Information on the number of sales and demolitions of social housing can be found in Live Tables 678 and 684 on gov.uk here.

The Social Housing Sales and Demolitions publication on gov.uk here includes commentary on these two types of disposals.

The release also includes a section of official statistics in development that uses data collected by my Department and the Regulator of Social Housing to estimate the net supply of social housing, including specifically all disposals for social rent undertaken by large private registered providers and local authorities with a Housing Revenue Account. This section is available for three years (2022-23 to 2024-25). Data for 2025-26 pre-announced for January/February can be found on gov.uk here.

Information on net supply is not available for rural areas, as the private registered provider information used is only available at England level.

The Social Housing Bill introduces a new requirement for private registered providers to notify other registered providers in a local area, including local authorities, before they can dispose of homes out of the regulated sector. At Commons’ Committee Stage, the government moved amendments to extend the notification period from four to eight weeks.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, what steps her Department is taking to reduce the time taken for applications to the Land Registry to change names or transfers of property on existing titles.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Improving speed of service remains a top priority for HM Land Registry (HMLR). Plans to achieve this are set out in the Agency’s Strategy 2025+ which was published on 5 November 2025 and can be found on gov.uk here.

As its sponsor department, the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government holds HMLR to account for its performance and operational delivery and is in regular communication with HMLR about their processing times.

HMLR continues to improve processing times by investing in its people and technology, increasing automation of simple application types, and improving the information received from customers through further pre-submission validation checks. HMLR is also developing the use of artificial intelligence to undertake administrative tasks.

The age of outstanding post-completion applications is now under nine months across all service lines, from a peak of 20 months in February 2023. In the first six months of 2026/27, HMLR completed over 338,000 more applications than in the same period last year.

HMLR processing times are publicly available on gov.uk here.

Anyone who is concerned that a delay to their application may cause financial, legal, or personal problems or put a property sale at risk, can apply to have their application expedited free of charge. HMLR processes nearly 1,400 expedited applications every day, with more than 95% actioned within 10 working days.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, further to the answer of 2 November 2026, to Questions 37649 and 36978, on Political Parties: Finance, what is the specific test that will be applied to determine whether an individual is UK resident for the purposes of the 6 July 2026 retrospective overseas contributors cap; and whether it will apply to domestic electors who have spent time overseas.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
For the purposes of the minimum residency period, the relevant requirement is that an individual has been UK resident throughout the applicable period. If they are not UK resident or were not UK resident at a point during the calendar year, the cap would apply for the remainder of the year in which they return to UK residency, and the following calendar year, from 1 January to 31 December.

Domestic electoral registration does not, in itself, establish that an individual is UK resident for the purposes of the overseas contributor cap. An individual who remains registered as a domestic elector may be subject to the cap if they have not been resident in the UK during the relevant period. Residency depends on the circumstances of the individual at the time of the donation.

The BSR has strengthened Gateway 3 processes, refining its approach using learning from the recent successful transformation of Gateway 2 performance. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps his Department is taking to support the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government’s ambition is for the UK to become the global destination of choice for next-generation financial markets by 2030, while maintaining appropriate standards of consumer protection and market integrity.

As set out at Mansion House 2026, HM Treasury is supporting the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets through a comprehensive programme of work, working alongside the Bank of England, Financial Conduct Authority and industry. This work has three strategic pillars: cryptoassets and stablecoins, next-generation payments, and the digitalisation of wholesale financial markets.

On cryptoassets, we have established a comprehensive regulatory regime, including stablecoins, due to take effect from October 2027.

On Payments, the Financial Services and Markets Bill currently before Parliament seeks to give the Bank of England a secondary innovation objective in relation to its regulation of systemic payment systems and digital settlement asset service providers. This will support the Government's aim for the UK to remain at the forefront of innovation in payments and digital finance.

On wholesale markets, our focus is on moving from experimentation to wider adoption. The Digital Securities Sandbox (DSS) provides a modified regulatory environment in which firms can undertake live digital-asset activity. Seventeen firms have entered the Sandbox, with three firms authorised to conduct live activity and further authorisations expected. The Government has also tabled an amendment to the Financial Services and Markets Bill that would allow HM Treasury to update specified legislation to reflect technological change in financial market infrastructure and support the adoption and scaling of digital assets and tokenised markets.

We are also supporting the development of the wider market infrastructure needed for adoption, including working towards delivering the pilot of the Digital Gilt Instrument (DIGIT), which is set to take place by Q1 2027. The government appointed Christopher Woolard CBE as Wholesale Digital Markets Champion. His first report, published in July 2026 sets out priorities and recommendations for developing the UK’s tokenised wholesale markets which are now being taken forward.
writtenQuestions.heading: Digital Assets: Regulation

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps he is taking to stimulate growth and job creation in high-skilled local industries across Leicester East constituency.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Reindustrialisation is central to the government’s plan to build a stronger, fairer, and more resilient economy. With the Modern Industrial Strategy at its heart, reindustrialisation will support good growth in every postcode. It will ensure that the UK is the best place for workers to build a career in thriving, globally competitive industries.

This government has already taken steps to tackle barriers to growth, including planning reform, removing the ban on the development of onshore wind farms and supporting local transport priorities with £59m of funding over 4 years (2026/27 – 2029/30) for Leicester via the Local Transport Grant.
At Budget 2026, the government confirmed it is now in the final stages of agreeing 10 new devolution agreements including a Mayoral Strategic Authority for Leicestershire, Leicester and Rutland. This will mean that Leicester can benefit from the reforms set out in the fiscal devolution roadmap, including income tax assignment and a direct share of business rates.  This will put regional government on a stronger long-term footing, ensuring places are rewarded for driving growth, whilst ensuring nowhere falls behind.

The Government is providing £60m over the next 10 years to Leicester through Pride in Place funding and providing an indicative £5.34m to support a Good Growth Fund in Leicestershire, Leicester and Rutland, giving local leaders greater flexibility to invest in their own growth priorities.

The government recognises that not all households struggling with their energy bills live in band A to D properties. That is why the government will provide an additional £100 million for local authorities to provide discretionary support to these households who are not eligible for the core rebate.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what regional modelling the Treasury has undertaken on the proportion of Scottish agricultural holdings and larger scale mixed family farms exceeding the £5 million combined spousal threshold for 100% Agricultural Property Relief, and what assessment has been made of the risk of forced land fragmentation or business dissolution across rural Scotland under the updated inheritance tax rules.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government continues to provide significant relief from inheritance tax for agricultural and business assets. A couple are able to pass on up to £5 million of such assets tax-free between them, on top of the existing allowances such as the nil-rate band.

Information from claims is not recorded to enable regional or national breakdowns of the number of estates expected to pay more inheritance tax due to the announced reforms to these reliefs. However, published information shows the reforms are expected to result in up to 185 estates across the UK claiming agricultural property relief, including those also claiming business property relief, paying more inheritance tax in 2026-27. This means around 85 per cent of estates claiming agricultural property relief, including those that also claim for business property relief, are forecast to not pay any more tax as a result of the changes in 2026-27. These estimates of the numbers of taxpayers are static and assume no change in behaviour, such as tax planning, which may reduce the numbers of estates affected. As such, these estimates should be viewed as a maximum.

The published tax information and impact note includes an assessment of the administrative impact on businesses and it is available at www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-agricultural-property-relief-and-business-property-relief/agricultural-property-relief-and-business-property-relief-changes. It is worth noting that Inheritance Tax only requires a valuation at a chargeable event, such as death, rather than an annual assessment.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps his Department is taking to tackle domestic enablers of illicit finance, in particular accounting and auditing services.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Tackling illicit finance and any professional enablers who facilitate it remains a key priority for this Government. Whilst the vast majority of professionals act as responsible gatekeepers, we recognise there are also complicit professional enablers who exploit the integrity of their professions to facilitate serious and organised crime and corruption. The Anti-Money Laundering and Asset Recovery Strategy sets out the Government's plan to intensify our response to this, including by investing in financial investigators, forensic accountants and cryptoasset capabilities.

The Government is also fundamentally reforming anti-money laundering supervision, including supervision of accounting and auditing services. This will support a more consistent, proportionate and effective approach and closer coordination with law enforcement, preventing UK professional services firms from being abused for illicit purposes.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the impact on households and businesses of their proposal to extend the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to refinery products; and what assessment they have made of the extent to which any additional costs may be passed on to consumers.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is an environmental measure designed to reduce the risk of carbon leakage by ensuring that highly traded, carbon-intensive goods imported into the UK face a carbon price comparable to that faced by UK producers.

At Budget 2026, the Government announced that it intends to expand the scope of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to include refinery products, subject to consultation on the feasibility and impacts of doing so.

The Government will confirm a timeline for implementation in due course, but we do not expect CBAM for refinery products to be in place for a few years, so there will be no impact on households or businesses in the short term.

The policy is designed to back British industry, by giving UK businesses the confidence to invest in decarbonisation, and prevent emissions, jobs and investment from being exported overseas.
writtenQuestions.heading: Refineries: UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the impact of the withdrawal of the VAT Retail Export Scheme on the UK fashion industry.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Recent external data shows a limited impact on the UK fashion industry as, tourism and spending have recovered at a similar rate following the pandemic to other European economies that offer tax-free shopping.

After adjusting each country’s tourism receipts for domestic inflation, UK receipts in 2024 recovered to around 111% of their 2019 level, compared with 107% in France, 117% in Spain, 103% in Italy and 83% in Germany.

The latest Office for Budget Responsibility’s assessment, which takes into account the indirect effects of the policy, estimated that the withdrawal of tax-free shopping will have saved the Exchequer around £540 million by 2025-26.
writtenQuestions.heading: Clothing: Exports

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government, further to the Written Answer by Lord Pitt-Watson on 2 November (HL4176), what they mean by “modest” liabilities arising from the introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The illustrative rates[1] published last month suggest a CBAM rate for iron and steel of £9.69/tCO₂e.

These rates are designed to help businesses prepare for the introduction of CBAM. Businesses can estimate potential liabilities by applying the relevant illustrative rate to actual emissions data or, where appropriate, the default value for a given product.

The CBAM rates applying for Q1 2027 will be published before the end of the year.

writtenStatements.title: UK National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing
writtenStatements.text:
My right honourable friend the Economic Secretary to the Treasury (Lucy Rigby) has today made the following statement:

The proliferation of chemical, biological and nuclear weapons poses a serious and evolving threat to the United Kingdom's national security and to the wider international community. Proliferation financing (PF) remains central to the ability of hostile states and networks to procure materials, technology and expertise in support of illicit weapons programmes.

As a global financial centre and trading hub, the UK is exposed to indirect and inherent PF risks. This updated National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing (PF NRA), published on 23 November 2026, sets out the Government's assessment of those threats and vulnerabilities, building on the UK's first PF NRA published in 2021. The publication fulfils the requirement under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (the MLRs) to maintain an up-to-date assessment of UK proliferation financing risks.

Produced by HM Treasury, with contributions from across government, supervisors, law enforcement and academic experts, the assessment provides an updated and evidence-based overview of the proliferation financing risks facing the UK. It reflects significant developments since 2021, including the increasing sophistication of sanctions evasion and procurement networks, the growing use of cryptoassets and cyber-enabled activity, and enhancements to the UK's counter-proliferation financing framework.

The key findings of the PF NRA are:

  1. The UK’s financial sector remains at high risk from proliferators. The assessment concludes that the UK's proliferation financing risk remains largely indirect and inadvertent, principally arising from the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) and Iran-linked procurement and financing networks. The UK's position as a major international financial, trading and shipping centre means that legitimate financial and commercial activity may be exploited by proliferators seeking to generate revenue, procure goods and technology, or evade sanctions. The assessment finds that banking and payments, trade finance providers, insurers, legal and professional service providers, and virtual asset service providers remain particularly exposed to proliferation financing risks. It also highlights emerging threats, including the use of cryptoassets, cyber-enabled activity and DPRK-linked remote IT workers to generate revenue and evade sanctions.
  2. The DPRK and Iran remain the most significant proliferation financing actors at state level. Both continue to rely on procurement and financing networks to evade sanctions, generate revenue and acquire goods, technology and expertise in support of their weapons programmes.
  3. Despite these threats, the 2026 assessment finds that the UK has continued to strengthen its strategic, regulatory and operational capabilities to counter proliferation financing. This includes updating relevant sanctions regimes, introducing new export controls and corporate transparency measures, and requiring firms regulated under the MLRs to identify, assess and mitigate PF risk. Together, these measures enhance the UK’s ability to detect, prevent and disrupt proliferation financing activity, while supporting firms, as the first line of defence, to apply proportionate and risk-based controls.

The report is available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-assessment-of-proliferation-financing-2026

This updated PF NRA demonstrates the UK's continued commitment to countering proliferation financing and protecting the integrity of the UK’s financial system. Since the publication of the first PF NRA in 2021, the UK has strengthened its counter-proliferation financing framework through enhancements to sanctions implementation and enforcement, export controls, corporate transparency and regulatory requirements on firms. The assessment supports the UK's wider national security objectives and reflects our continued leadership in international efforts to improve understanding of PF risks and strengthen implementation of Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.
